newsitem.title: INDIA: Pro-Sikh party wins Punjab state polls.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Sikh party wins Punjab state polls.

text.p: A pro-Sikh regional party and its Hindu nationalist ally, promising religious harmony and peace in India's agricultural hub, won a clear majority in local polls in the troubled state of Punjab on Sunday.

Officials said the predominantly Sikh Akali Dal party of former state chief minister Prakash Singh Badal won 45 seats in the 117-member state assembly out of the 73 results declared so far. The party was leading in 27 other seats.
India's main opposition rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won 14 seats and was leading in five.
"The Akali Dal-BJP alliance have gained a clear majority," Punjab's chief election official Brajendra Singh told Reuters in the state capital of Chandigarh.
India's Congress party, which had ruled the state since 1992, conceded defeat but said democracy had returned to the region because of the party's sustained efforts.
"I would like to concede victory to the Akali Dal," Congress general secretary Ghulam Nabi Azad told state-run Doordarshan television. "We may have lost, but the democracy has won."
The Congress party, which won 87 seats in the 1992 state polls boycotted by the Dal, won seven seats and a pro-separatist faction of Akali Dal which fielded 29 candidates had just a single seat.
Akali Dal's former interior minister Kanwaljit Singh told Reuters his party had shifted its focus from the welfare of the state's majority Sikhs to friendship with its Hindus.
"Hindus may be in a minority in Punjab, but we have realised that the state cannot progress without their total involvement in its governance," he said.
More than 68 percent of Punjab's 15 million voters turned out on Friday in a remarkably peaceful election. The polls were the first in two decades not to be overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence.
But officials said the state's political groups were too badly divided to ensure badly-needed stability.
The Akali Dal's poll alliance with the BJP was seen as offering a chance to Punjab's two main communities -- Hindus and Sikhs -- to overcome their mistrust, analysts said.
"These elections will prove to be a triumph for Punjabi unity," said Balramji Das Tandon, a BJP candidate in the Rajpura constitency.
The state Congress party, led by its first woman chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, claims credit for the virtual weeding out of Sikh militancy from the region.
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.
